The rise of pretrained language models has spurred significant advancements in long-document ranking. While recent research addresses this by extracting substantial textual signals from the structural features inherent in documents, current methods often struggle to effectively leverage document structure. To mitigate these limitations, we present a novel approach termed "document bag sampling." This technique randomly partitions textual signals extracted from a document into distinct groups, or "bags." Each query document is thus represented by its corresponding bags sampled during preprocessing. Subsequently, we utilize the CLS token from the last hidden state of each bag to form a bag-specific representation vector. Experimental results demonstrate that this sampling strategy enhances long-document ranking accuracy. We have integrated this method into recent architectures—specifically MultiBERT and T5-Encoder—yielding improvements of 2.6% and 2.1%, respectively, on the DuORC dataset. Furthermore, our method exhibits robustness across various model architectures and hyperparameter settings. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/multimodal-summarization/tree/master/bag_sampling.

This study investigates how the pseudo-labeling procedure affects the performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in a semi-supervised node classification setting. We pinpoint the specific stages within this pipeline that undermine GNN performance and introduce a simple yet robust alternation in the labeling step that significantly improves outcomes. Our proposed approach is straightforward to implement and integrates easily with any standard semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method by adapting it with two distinct techniques: we suggest an improved method for determining the confidence of node labels and present an innovative strategy for balancing class proportions during the pseudo-labeling process by leveraging the bipartite matching concept. Experiments across various graph datasets confirm that the effectiveness of our approach is both robust across different network structures and insensitive to variations in hyperparameters.

This study examines how radial size variations affect beam propagation during beam-driven plasma wakefield acceleration involving betatron radiation. Our approach utilizes a 2.5D full-wave code, OP3, which self-consistently solves the coupled equations for electromagnetic fields, particle dynamics, and the vapor plasma medium. Two acceleration scenarios based on a hollow-gas jet were analyzed: the first maintains a constant electron beam radius while the channel gas remains uniform, whereas the second introduces gradual expansions in the electron beam radius relative to the jet. Our observations indicate that, during the acceleration process, transverse size mismatches—whether caused by the initial setup or the relative growth between the channel and the beam—significantly affect the evolution of the radiated spectrum. Specifically, radial expansion of the electron beam within a shrinking plasma channel can induce a high-energy cutoff in the emission spectrum. Consequently, achieving an effective betatron radiation betatron requires precise matching between initial transverse sizes and a controlled evolution of their size ratio throughout the acceleration stage.

These findings demonstrate that even with the constraints of differential privacy applied to tree structures, high-quality and competitive models can be developed. Ultimately, our data suggests that differentially private decision trees become increasingly effective as training data scales.

We present novel product Dirichlet priors designed for selecting models within chain event graphs—a framework employed across epidemiology, social science, and operational research to trace intricate, stepwise processes. This article examines an extensive class of games where players strive to minimize a cost dependent on both their own decisions and those of others, a scenario where optimal strategies are defined by the Pontryagin principle. Although the authors established that Nash equilibria in these games generally cannot be explicitly formulated, a specific sub-category was identified for which a clear Nash equilibrium can be derived. The theoretical framework is then applied to analyze vehicle platooning, a setting where the dynamics depend on surrounding cars. In this context, vehicle spacing is maintained by adjusting relative accelerations, and we demonstrate that the identified Nash equilibrium results in uniform time-based headways. Furthermore, we show that as Platoons increase in size, the enhanced stability of their strategies allows for strictly diminished inter-vehicle temporal distances compared to previous approaches.

Recent research examining the capabilities of transformer models has investigated the ability of both humans to identify AI-written versus human-authored text and, conversely, the ability of AI systems to mimic human writing effectively. This paper presents new experimental findings derived from a dataset comprising approximately 1,000,000 headlines to evaluate these two specific aspects. Analysis reveals that transformer models are highly proficient at generating headlines that are difficult for humans to distinguish from those created by humans. In contrast, human ability to differentiate between AI and human construction of headlines is largely unreliable; specifically, models achieve approximately 90% detection accuracy, while humans achieve around 44%. Although model-based detection is generally more accurate than human judgment, the study indicates that models fail to consistently outperform humans when their accuracy drops below certain thresholds. These results suggest that AI systems achieve greater success in producing text that escapes human identification, effectively demonstrating a higher rate of successful text imitation in such specialized domains.

We theoretically investigate chiral spin liquids in kagome antiferromagnets, focusing on a microscopic Hubbard model that features strong electron correlations alongside significant electron and spin interactions. Because of their uncertainty modeling capabilities via stochasticity, Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) have garnered significant attention for achieving robust classification, particularly when confronting small and noisy datasets. However, this stochastic uncertainty is often unnecessary when dealing with large training sets in well-defined regimes, where conventional deterministic neural networks (NNs) outperform BNNs in handling balanced data with superior speed, accuracy, and generalization, rendering them effectively equivalent. Conversely, in highly imbalanced regimes, the cost of stochastic uncertainty and the complexity of training BNNs become prohibitive. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework that eliminates stochasticity by introducing a regularization term inspired by the variational free energy of Bayesian posterior distributions. We demonstrate that this penalty successfully suppresses stochastic uncertainty and effectively regularizes both standard NNs and gradient boosting regressors, enabling them to match BNNs in handling imbalanced data with superior performance metrics. Specifically, our proposed method achieves on par accuracy and generalization capabilities as BNNs but with substantially enhanced training efficiency and inference speed, establishing a robust framework for addressing imbalanced classification tasks.

User-generated content (UGC) on social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram is easily accessible, but locating specific information within this vast sea of data is challenging. While current search engines rely on users crafting detailed boolean queries or utilizing tag-based systems, these approaches are often too complex or labor-intensive for the average person. To address this, this paper introduces "TwitterSearcher," a system designed to simplify UGC access by enabling users to formulate natural language search queries for Twitter. This tool was developed by automatically learning effective search terms from users' query histories. By optimizing for relevance through techniques like learning to rank and term relevance, the system adapts to individual search habits. A pivotal innovation is a new relevance metric that accounts for the frequency of specific keywords within the users' query sets. By automatically generating optimized searches based on a user's own query history, the search engine suggests refined queries that automatically filter out irrelevant results. User tests revealed that the system successfully enhanced the precision of suggested queries, and a broader study demonstrated that these automatic suggestions boost both the precision and recall of searching specific topics.

Adiabatic dynamics in moist air are governed by the competing effects of latent heat and radiative cooling alongside gas expansion. However, the standard thermodynamic equations of state remain under a crucial constraint: the need to consistently integrate mass and energy conservation with the radiative cooling rate. We demonstrate that the constant $\kappa$ approach offers a consistent and practical solution for describing the cooling rate of the atmosphere. This concept has not been thoroughly explored in current literature. We provide numerical verification proving that the $\kappa$ method accurately reproduces the radiative cooling rate of the atmosphere under specific conditions. Moreover, we show that the method accurately predicts the temperature profile when the atmosphere transitions from dry to humid. This approach allows for straightforward calculation of the rate without resorting to complex numerical integration methods.

Entanglement serves as a critical resource for a wide array of tasks, including metrology and fundamental physics. Obtaining precise estimates of this resource demands the application of optimal estimators, the implementation of which facilitates the discrimination of diverse decoherence models associated with noise. In this study, this approach is investigated through two specific scenarios: first, estimating linear coherence in phase estimation using noisy qubits subject to the $Z$-rotation generator; second, determining linear entanglement in multi-partite Greenberger-Horne-Zeyn (GHZ) states affected by qutrits undergoing $T$ and $T$ processes. Furthermore, the robustness of linear coherence in $Z$ decoherence and linear entanglement in $T$ decoherence was observed in both analyzed cases. This study introduces a theoretical framework to explain experimental observations of newly identified palm tree modes (PTMs) in the DIII-D tokamak. The mechanism relies on the coupling between a non-axisymmetric mode and an edge localized magnetic island. This paper introduces "NMC-Continual," a simple yet effective approach to continual learning based on a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). Sociocultural context is a vital element for identifying hate speech. However, deep learning models trained on unstructured textual data often excel at spotting discourses targeting groups based on conventional characteristics like religion, race, or nationality, while frequently failing to address context-laden issues related to sex, age, or culinary preferences. To tackle this shortfall, we introduce a Context-Hate dataset featuring statements about cilantro that include or exclude additional content targeting various identity groups alongside distinct labels indicating the level of hate. Although machine learning (ML) is transforming the management of personal data in healthcare, it has attracted limited scholarly attention regarding security. This study addresses this gap by examining how AI and ML enhance the protection of personal health information within the healthcare sector. By integrating the concept of computer security more closely with ML and IoT technologies, the framework minimizes the risk of data leakage and the overall impact if incidents occur. Security protocols are developed through machine learning algorithms that analyze interactions between users and systems to identify anomalies and potential attacks. These algorithms build user behavioral models to verify legitimacy, while a classifier system flags suspicious activities for immediate alerting. The robustness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has drawn significant attention recently due to their ability to deliver reliable predictions despite noise. This paper examines decentralized GNNs within wireless communication systems, where training occurs locally on user devices and a global model is aggregated via multi-user cooperation. Consequently, the final global model's performance depends on the exchange of intermediate states among users. However, this interaction introduces potential non-IID data and noise robustness issues. The primary objective is to analyze the noise resilience of this decentralized framework. To achieve this, the paper investigates the impact of stochasticity on convergence under Asynchronous Distributed Stochastic Edge Convolution (A-DES-ES), an iterative, message-passing based decentralized GNN algorithm. To this end, the paper presents a comprehensive stochastic convergence analysis of the system. Furthermore, the paper introduces a normalization-based approach to enhance the robustness of the resulting global model's inferences against non-IID data distribution and system noise. Finally, the paper validates these theoretical findings through experiments comparing the proposed algorithms against multiple baselines.

Homicide is a pervasive global concern that significantly impacts societal well-being. This research investigates the determinants of homicide rates in the United States, specifically examining whether large urban centers exert a spatial influence on surrounding areas. By analyzing panel data from 2002 to 2012, the study applies a spatial panel model and evaluates various socioeconomic indicators and their spatial dynamics. The analysis reveals that both rural and city environments experience higher homicide rates when surrounded by similar neighborhoods, yet it highlights a distinct dynamic in larger cities: while they do not automatically elevate homicide in adjacent regions, they do attract a reduction in local rates in broader areas, and larger metropolitan areas with higher initial homicide levels tend to see decreased rates subsequently. Furthermore, despite the tendency for urbanization to initially raise costs, increased density ultimately produces a net decrease in homicides.

We investigate the application of Nesterov acceleration to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) within the presence of adaptive step-sizes. We demonstrate that the ergodic sequence of iterations converges at an $	ext{O}(1/√t)$ rate in the non-convex setting and achieves $	ext{O}(√(log(1/ε)))$ rates for convex objectives. These results are significant as they represent the first proofs of accelerated performance for general adaptive step-sizes; notably, prior to this, accelerated methods had only been established in specific cases, such as non-uniformly bounded variance or heavy-tailed gradients. Furthermore, our methodology offers insights applicable to continuous-time ordinary differential equations and the analysis of adaptive step-sizes.

The recent Fermi-LAT detection of diffuse gamma-ray emissions from the Galactic Center motivates an investigation into whether this signal can arise from the annihilation of light particles, such as axions or ALPs (ALPs), given by a galactic dark matter (DM) distribution. This study focuses on establishing constraints for such ALPs within the framework of the "local local" setup. We specifically aim to delineate the viable parameter space where the Galactic Center's diffuse emission results from $a \to \gamma \gamma$ processes, utilizing energy scales and axion-phobic couplings that ALPs acquire from QCD forces. We also assess axion DM density limits arising from stellar evolution and laboratory experiments.

By coupling a bosonic oscillator to two thermal reservoirs at distinct temperatures, one can mimic the behavior of nonlinear self-oscillating systems previously shown to generate time-periodic motion when a threshold temperature difference is met. This approach generates a mean-field description that captures a similar threshold effect, where a non-zero coherent state emerges. The corresponding dynamics are captured by a Lindblad master equation featuring a coherent coupling term between states separated by an excitation gap and dissipative terms that bridge temperature-dependent states. Finally, within the quantum regime, the mean-field approximation is refined by incorporating quantum fluctuations as corrections. This work further details how quantum fluctuations influence spectral properties and clarify conditions under which the simple mean-field approach remains valid.

We introduce DexGraspNet, an end-to-end neural network capable of synthesizing diverse and stable grasps for a seven-finger Amazon Robotics Arm Grasper. Utilizing a novel volume-based differentiable grasp simulator, we achieve efficient backpropagation to filter out unstable and infeasible grasps from our training data, thereby ensuring high-quality synthetic examples. To enhance training efficiency and reduce the computational burden of sampling, we employ an innovative sequential two-stage sampling approach; this method significantly increases the probability of sampling viable and stable grasps while allowing the generation of full-grasping trajectory data (used for execution and refinement) exclusively for the most stable samples. Empirical results show that the synthesized data outperforms prior synthetic benchmarks, such as GraspNet, in both real-world and simulated domains, yielding notably better zero-shot generalization. Additionally, we demonstrate that our synthetic data facilitates the training of a state-of-the-art grasp recommendation model and an object placement network, both of which achieve marked performance gains.

This study introduces a novel Sampling pattern for Spatial Spectrometers, termed rCASPR (random circular sparse), designed for use in Fourier Spectrometers. The method involves sampling the aperture with non-linear circular clusters of pixels. The approach was evaluated using both simulations and empirical validation within the Fourier Spectrometers, demonstrating that rCASPR yields a point-spread function that closely approximates a Gaussian profile, alongside higher image contrast and more uniform spectral resolution compared to linear sampling. Furthermore, the numerical analysis indicates that rCASPR achieves these optimal characteristics across the Spectrometers regardless of the density level, even outperforming linear arrays at equivalent sampling rates.

This paper introduces **AdaPrune**, a novel and efficient channel pruning method designed to handle the information transfer challenges between teacher and student models. The approach features adaptive pruning that adapts to varying network depths and propagation layers within the teacher model. The core of the proposed method is a dedicated loss function that guides the transfer of channel information by inducing correlation among channel coefficients across different spatial locations. This technique effectively reduces inter-channel redundancy, with a side effect that main channels become more expressive. The authors demonstrate that AdaPrune can reduce a ResNet-50 model to 44% of its original FLOPs while maintaining 49.8% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet dataset.

The findings indicate that the system becomes more unstable as the pattern of animal distribution shifts from localized to nonlocal forms.

This paper introduces a demand structure-independent auction mechanism for selling $n$ items across $m$ time periods. The approach combines the supply structure of a dynamic auction with the objective function found in multi-item multi-period auctions. The core objective is for the seller to maximize expected revenue, while buyers act to minimize total costs, which include both acquisition costs and switching costs incurred when changing from one set of items to another in each period. The paper first establishes a new auction mechanism and subsequently proves that, regardless of the specific demand structure applied, both supply and switching costs result in a guaranteed minimum of a $\min\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{n}\right)$-approximation of optimal expected revenue for the seller. Furthermore, three additional approximation guarantees are derived based on specific assumptions regarding the cost functions. Finally, an approximation ratio is also proven when considering a generalized model involving a more flexible cost structure for both buyers and sellers.

Entity-based summaries are essential for condensing long documents into concise forms, yet existing abstractive systems often produce inaccurate readings of document facts. This study addresses this flaw by utilizing "entity chains"—ordered sequences of entities that capture the document's information structure and serve as a natural summary control mechanism—to constrain output precision. The authors introduce a novel framework that leverages these chains to suppress factual errors, evaluated on the XSum and SX-880 datasets where their approach achieved an approximate 3% improvement in entity precision over current best methods. Source code is available at https://github.com/tao-liu-lin/SummER.

This paper demonstrates how the differential properties, specifically differentiability, of a function depending on n variables can be linked to that of a function depending on n-1 variables. As a practical application, we present an algorithm with time complexity O(n) designed to compute a formal differential for an n-variable function formally drawn from a specified set.

While social entrainment is a hallmark feature of social interaction in the general population, individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) frequently demonstrate compromised entrainment behaviors. This study proposes a new approach to characterizing both the degree of vocal entrainment and the specific patterns associated with it in the speech produced by individuals with ASD and typically developing (TD) control participants. The methodology involves applying state-space modeling to simultaneously capture attributes such as the level of entrainment and its dynamic oscillation dynamics. These models are applied to a dataset comprising "Think, Share, Care" interviews, during which pairs viewed videos and alternated speaking, taking turns. Results indicate that while TD pairs generally exhibit stronger vocal synchrony and a higher frequency of silent periods (pauses), individuals with ASD conversational pairs show distinct dynamics characterized by less synchronization and more frequent pauses compared to the TD control. Importantly, the analysis reveals that while entrainment levels differ between groups, both ASD and TD groups react to changes in synchrony in parallel, maintaining a stable offset rather than altering their underlying dynamic structure when entrainment decreases. These findings demonstrate the utility of the proposed analytical framework in both differentiating groups and offering a process-level understanding of how conversations evolve over time.

Two distinct approaches to resolving this inequality are proposed and evaluated: a non-conservative strategy that simplifies physics for tractability, and a conservative approach that maintains physical fidelity but renders mathematical analysis more challenging.

Ionised gas outflows are a recognized phenomenon in disk galaxies, yet their impact on the observed gas depletion timescales remains uncertain. This study investigates the relationship between outflows and the star-formation timescale by integrating deep, narrow-band imaging data from the 3.9$\mu$m band with existing star-forming rate estimates for the COSMOS field. The sample comprises approximately 150 star-forming disk galaxies with star-formation rates (SFR) exceeding 0.1 M$_{\odot} yr^{-1}$ at redshifts ranging from z=0.3 to z=2.4. For each galaxy, we calculated the extended outflowing gas mass by measuring the spatially resolved escape velocities of the outflows. The analysis reveals that in gas-rich star-forming disks, gas timescales elongate with increasing redshifts up to z=2, mirroring cosmic star-formation rate density trends. The strongest drivers for this shift are gas accretion from the intergalactic medium and intrinsic galactic outflows. The latter can account for up to 40% of the observed increase in gas timescales. Furthermore, the mean extended gas escape velocities are found to be 20 km s$^{-1}$ at z=0.6 and 30 km s$^{-1}$ at z=1.5, a rate sufficient to explain a significant portion of the cosmic star-formation rate density rise.

Specifically, for distributions possessing a fixed graphical structure, we present methods with runtime complexity linear in the number of observations and polynomial in the number of variables, alongside algorithms with sublinear time complexity relative to sample sizes that remain applicable to arbitrary dependence structures among $n$ observations. Additionally, we demonstrate how the primary framework facilitates the computation of optimal transport costs between functions and the derivation of corresponding gradients and subgradients. We further establish the convexity of Kendall's tau with respect to distribution parameters and provide valid lower bounds. The proposed methodologies are applied to address the challenges of maximum likelihood and empirical Bayes estimation when approximating Kendall's tau.

Additionally, we evaluate the performance of our method against existing attacks and the accuracy and efficiency gains relative to baseline approaches under realistic constraints. Our work offers critical insights for enhancing the security of decentralized machine learning paradigms.

The development of multi-scale and multi-frame algorithms for image segmentation addresses the challenge of handling severely degraded input data. This study introduces an adaptive generalization of the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah framework to tackle the issue of image corruption more effectively than previous approaches. The proposed method utilizes an optimized total variation-based prior that functions as a segment-dependent, non-convex regularization term. The resulting model is resolved through an alternating minimization strategy combining the split Bregman technique with a novel partial differential equation (PDE) gradient flow method. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is validated through both benchmark and real-world experiments, demonstrating its superior ability in segmenting images contaminated by noise and structural cracks compared to existing methodologies.

Perovskites are renowned for their rich structural diversity and exceptional functional properties. Although photoexcitation is a well-studied phenomenon in this material class, its influence on emergent topological phonons has received little attention. In this study, we investigate tetragonal K0.5Na0.5BiO3, a system that supports both trivial and topologically non-trivial phonon bands depending on whether it is in its ground state or locally excited. Specifically, pump-probe experiments reveal that photoexcitation triggers thermal softening of specific lattice modes, causing the phase transition to a topologically non-trivial topological phonon state characterized by surface modes. Furthermore, we examine alterations in the bulk and surface phonon spectra by analyzing the wavevector-dependent acoustic response. These findings provide a pathway to dynamically and controllably manipulate topological phonons in superconducting perovskites using light.

Real-time anomaly detection remains challenging, particularly for large datasets where maintaining excessive computational overhead for neighbor searches hinders the application of proximity-based methods. Although RandProJ, an existing random-point graph approach, addresses outlying by constructing a sparse connectivity structure, the study identifies two key limitations: the graph is not fully sparse, leading to unnecessary overhead, and the risk of generating disconnected components. To resolve these issues, we introduce the Memory Representation Point Graph (MRPG), designed to create a truly sparse and well-connected structure tailored for efficient anomaly detection. Specifically, we present a novel MRPG-based anomaly detection algorithm that outperforms existing techniques, including RandProJ. Experimental validation across various datasets confirms our approach is not only superior in accuracy but achieves a significant speedup—up to 100 times faster—thereby enabling the processing of previously intractable datasets. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that MRPG facilitates the creation of more efficient and effective anomaly detection graphs.

We investigate the emission and scattering of photons by a moving neutral atom near a mirror using quantum electrodynamics in the Coulomb gauge. This approach integrates the atomic dipole interaction with the transverse electromagnetic field while ensuring Galilean invariance through the specific inclusion of a Hermitian, time-derivative term. This term facilitates the proper coupling between the electric field and the atomic momentum. By applying perturbation theory, an expression for the emission rate is derived. This result encompasses the mirror-induced changes to spontaneous emission, including multi-photon exchange processes, as well as the conditions under which this emission remains consistent with the principle of optical reciprocity.

Graph Representation Learning (GRL) aims to map nodes to a latent space optimized for specific downstream tasks by leveraging graph structure and auxiliary attributes. However, results from recent studies on pre-training for graph attribute classification reveal performance biases towards certain groups, specifically due to imbalanced node distributions within their neighborhoods. To address this, this work introduces a simple yet effective node embedding technique that ensures neighborhood fairness, thereby reducing such biases. Empirical evaluations across various graphs and downstream tasks, analyzed both with and without attribute data, demonstrate that the proposed method significantly boosts accuracy in tasks affected by bias. Furthermore, experiments indicate that explicitly modeling neighborhoods leads to a substantial reduction in disparities in error rates. Interestingly, these findings suggest an inverse relationship between bias and the overall average accuracy in the tested datasets.

We introduce a technique for the LHC detection of long-lived gluinos that utilize the full information contained within jet structures. The approach utilizes the distance from reconstructed particle vertices to these associated jets to estimate decay length and investigates the gluino's impact on these metrics. A search for gluinos with decay lengths extending from sub-millimeter to several meters is conducted using the full 13 TeV LHC dataset comprising 137 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected in 2015-2016. The study evaluates decay channels with decay lengths ranging from 0.1 micrometers to 5 meters, comparing fixed-length buckets with continuous sensitivity. Search strategies are evaluated using both the standard fixed-bucket approach and a novel method to reconstruct decay length from the reconstructed tracks of particles within jets. This latter approach aims to enhance the gluino's sensitivity, particularly in regimes where the decay occurs within the calorimeter or the inner tracker of the detector.

Financial bubbles are frequent occurrences that eventually burst, often driven by nonlinear feedback dynamics. This study employs a multilayer agent-based framework featuring a nonlinear feedback mechanism to model these bubbles and their crashes. We utilize a two-layer network with two interacting cases: a positive feedback loop, which is consistent with financial theories, and a negative feedback loop, which acts as a deflationary force. Each agent functions as a mean-reverting or non-mean-reverting investor; among non-mean-reverting agents, we select a fraction with bubble-prone behavior. We find that the two-layer architecture facilitates more extreme price spikes compared to a single-layer model. The interaction between layers significantly influences the duration of the bubble's expansion phase and the intensity of the crash that follows. Moreover, the termination of financial bubbles is not a linear trajectory but is instead driven by the cross-layer interference affecting both time dynamics and the magnitude of the peak.

We investigate a monochromatically driven Rabi model, a framework encompassing various spinboson systems, analyzing both its classical energy-coherent quantum counterparts. As coherent states represent the optimal localized description for driven quantum environments, we examine the interplay between classical trajectories and quantum dynamics under these conditions. Our analysis extends beyond the weak-coupling limit typically assumed in quantum optics for slowly varying envelopes to include sudden switch-on scenarios. We uncover that while classical motion remains regular, specific parameter regimes induce chaotic behavior in coherent state evolution. This complexity arises intrinsically from the coupling between spin and bosonic degrees of freedom and persists regardless of switching speed. In summary, the radiation damping driving the coherent states is a crucial factor that can amplify existing classical regular motions into quantum chaos.

Black hole X-ray transients (BHTRs) are known to exhibit Type-A, B, and C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs), yet the physical mechanisms driving Type-C QPOs remain elusive. This study investigates the origin of Type-C QPOs by analyzing 17 black hole X-ray binary flare events identified in the Swift archive. By calculating the time-resolved spectral hardness ratios, we identified 17 such events displaying hard-soft transitions and accompanied by Type-C QPOs. Observations indicate a rising frequency of Type-C QPOs during the hard-intermediate phase; furthermore, the post-flare X-ray continuum and iron K$\alpha$ lines generally lack these QPO signals. By utilizing the Novikov-Thorne model to fit iron line profiles across pre-, peak, and post-flare intervals, we aimed to discern structural changes in the accretion disk. While no definitive evidence for such changes emerged, the post-flare inner disk radius was notably smaller than the pre-flure one in 11 out of 17 cases. Additionally, the frequency of post-flare Type-C QPOs shows an inverse correlation with the post-flare inner disk radius. These findings suggest that accretion-driven disk shrinking may underpin the generation of Type-C QPOs in black hole X-ray transients.

A critical factor in designing effective multi-agent learning systems is the rate at which agents acquire knowledge. Building upon recent findings regarding environmental "pull" forces that attract agents to certain states, this study investigates a corresponding concept termed "transfer empowerment." This concept represents an agent's push dynamics, reflecting its capacity to reposition the environment. By analyzing the relationship between these opposing forces—pull (current value) and push (future adaptability)—we can better evaluate learning efficiency. We demonstrate that this transfer property of the environment significantly influences multi-agent reinforcement learning. Specifically, agents capable of balancing pull and push forces achieve higher levels of cooperation and exhibit faster improvement rates. We also show that traditional single-agent models serve as a subset of general multi-agent problems. Consequently, established measures of complexity in this domain, such as entropy capacity and vacuum levels, are identified as subsets of what transfer empowerment encompasses within the multi-agent context. Finally, we present results from simulations across various cooperative tasks, illustrating that agents equipped with learned transfer empowerment metrics outperform those relying solely on standard state value estimates.

Notably, the system successfully achieved 86% identification accuracy for new material classes despite being trained on just five seconds of video per class.

Morphological typology categorizes the world's languages by contrasting structural features like word order, phrasal alignment, and inflection. Our findings indicate that measures of morphological complexity are more strongly associated with inflection than with other typological aspects. Furthermore, the distribution of complexity scores is highly skewed, resulting in extensive overlap between high and low levels across different metrics. Galaxy cluster substructures are a key component of both X-ray and millimeter-wave emissions, and they significantly impact gravitational lensing models, which are a primary method for measuring cluster mass. Baryons, by gravitating more centrally, distort the lensing analysis, creating a discrepancy between the total gravitational mass and the data-driven mass that can exceed 10% in certain scenarios. We examine this discrepancy across a sample of 20 lensing cluster substructures, utilizing high-resolution X-ray and millimeter-wave continuum datasets to profile the mass distribution. By comparing these substructures against high-resolution N-body simulations of cosmic web filaments, we find that the discrepancy between gravitational mass and lensing-based mass correlates with the degree of baryonic concentration. Specifically, in systems with high baryon concentration, the mismatch reaches up to 20%, whereas lower concentration results in mismatches as low as 5%. Baryon concentration in these cases is linked to the presence of hot gas filaments connecting dense regions within the cosmic web. Our findings indicate that the mass discrepancy is not driven by baryons collapsing toward the center, but rather by cluster substructures becoming more elongated along the filament axis. Consequently, in future studies utilizing substructures as cosmic probes, accounting for the specific geometry of each substructure will be essential.

Kernel Fisher Discriminant Analysis (KFD) serves as a powerful non-linear extension of Fisher Discriminant Analysis, designed for efficient handling of high-dimensional datasets. Furthermore, the function's parameters are tuned using an adaptive strategy based on the Gaussian distribution. Comprehensive experiments conducted on various datasets confirm that the m-AKF-driven KFD outperforms both standard KFD and other state-of-the-art dimensionality reduction techniques.

This approach ensures that the expert's domain knowledge is fully integrated into the model architecture rather than being overridden by it alone. Validation against a large-scale A/B test demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in business metrics, with results that are both statistically and practically meaningful.

We investigate a restricted model featuring a barrier, where the population count in a compact region evolves via a subcritical or supercritical branching process, with each individual producing mutations. Unlike standard branching processes with random mutations, here a "ladder process" tracks the highest mutation level that has reached a specific genetic "height." Our main goal is to clarify the relationship between this ladder process and the underlying particle system. This framework offers valuable insights into coalescing particle systems and branching diffusion systems with selection, particularly within critical or near-critical regimes. In the latter case, selection favors the most highly mutated particles, with fitness increasing as a sublinear super-exponent of the mutation count. This setup serves as a discrete approximation of a super-exponential diffusion system with selection.

To simulate delayed coherent quantum feedback, a single quantum in a lossless waveguide is coupled with a second transverse quantum under the influence of non-Markovian bath conditions. By analyzing an arbitrary qubit of this system, we map out scattering matrix parameters related to N-photon processes. Such feedback mechanisms allow us generate sophisticated quantum states, implement gates within quantum computing, and achieve control over coherence. We show that an initially parametrically independent set of scattering amplitudes, resulting from perfect memory in the bath, can be reduced to a two-parameter representation. Furthermore, we explore how N-photon interactions are affected by the emergence of entanglement between incoming photons, which serves as a resource for their manipulation.

This research investigates boosted dark matter (DM) serving as a novel spin-dependent interaction model at sub-GeV mass scales, targeting the Nucleus for Experiments with Light (NEXUS) detector. We evaluate the feasibility of achieving sensitivity within NEXEX's design goals and demonstrate that the DM-nucleus cross-section probed by DM-nucleus scattering can reach levels comparable to those of standard contact interactions. Specifically, we show NEXEX could probe spin-dependent sub-GeV DM-nucleus cross-sections up to approximately $10^{-27}~{\rm cm}^2$, outperforming existing direct detection experiments like CRESST III and SuperCDMS by orders of magnitude. Additionally, we incorporate constraints from muon spin precession, astrophysical observations, and relic abundance data to evaluate NEXEX's exclusion reach for both thermal and non-thermal DM scenarios.

The application of continuous phase modulation (CPM) signals across next-generation communication systems is increasing. While conventional differential detection (DD) remains popular due to its simplicity and lack of required pilot signals, it suffers from a high bit error rate (BER). The proposed method matches the performance of a maximum likelihood sequence estimator at the same signal-to-noise ratio but operates with much lower computational burden. Furthermore, this proposed constellation can be utilized with other detection schemes to yield similar performance gains.

This study examines how noncommutative effects influence the consistency between theoretical predictions and experimental data for nucleon structure functions within the regime of small $x_{BJ}$ values. This study examines how the interaction between nonlinearity and frustration influences the topological order of the 1+D entanglement spectrum in a frustrated bilinear-biquadratic spin chain, specifically for ground states characterized by low or mid-range anisotropy. We discover a complex dynamic where nonlinearity and frustration mutually generate fresh phases and cause the recovery of existing ones marked by restored topological order. It is crucial to highlight that, in this specific system, the persistent destruction of topological order is not solely the result of frustration; rather, it results from the intricate relationship between both effects. The phase transitions within this nonlinear system were further analyzed using classical perturbation theory applied to the bilinear form, offering insights comparable to those derived from a fully bilinear framework. Ultimately, our numerical verification demonstrates the robust nature and significance of these phase shifts, confirming their persistence even under minor ground state perturbations.

While numerous methods have been developed to decipher the internal mechanisms of models, confidence in their reliability remains inconsistent. Researchers analyzing extreme events in real-world datasets frequently rely on Bayesian methods using truncated power laws as estimators. A critical tuning parameter, denoted as $m$, determines the cutoff that separates the data's body from its tail. This study examines various approaches for estimating $m$ that avoid the subjectivity of selection. We evaluate multiple metrics for model fit and external validation while analyzing the impact of different estimators. Our results indicate that models employing Bayesian measures and validation criteria often perform similarly to those using Bayesian information and Akaike criteria, sharing certain limitations. Consequently, we advocate utilizing the mean squared posterior predictive accuracy for selecting an appropriate model, particularly because it functions independently of specific test metrics. Furthermore, across both simulation studies and practical applications involving real data, these findings hold true.

This study investigates the derivation of physical laws for the speed-accuracy trade-off, which links movement velocity and precision, as demonstrated by the relationship between displacement and speed in one-dimensional systems. We propose a new physical law, the "speed-decay of accuracy," which posits that the mean-square displacement (MSD) of a particle in physical space is a function solely of the mean-square displacement of the same particle in a configurational space. By utilizing this principle, we can bridge the gap between physical laws and the optimization of precision and speed in both biological organisms and artificial agents. Consequently, this framework also sheds a novel perspective on the conservation of the particle's mean-square displacement of physical space when its speed is held constant. Furthermore we introduce an approach that allows us to demonstrate the validity of the proposed law.

We conducted a laboratory experiment to measure the transmission of Lyman-$\alpha$ radiation through a molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) absorption cell, specifically aiming to understand how cell pressure and the photon incident angle influence absorption. By comparing experimental data (at a constant 10 mTorr H$_2$ pressure) with theoretical models, we identified significant deviations at the absorption line center, which are attributed to the neglect of pressure-broadened H$_2$ Lyman-$\alpha$ line profiles in current models. Our analysis reveals increased absorption at the line center as pressure rises, demonstrating that the filter effect can be adjusted by adjusting the H$_2$ pressure. Additionally, we found that Lyman-$\alpha$ photons undergo substantial redistribution as they traverse the absorption profile due to resonant scattering. This phenomenon implies that, at the very center of the line profile, the scattering cross-section can reach up to 100 times the resonant line width. Our findings demonstrate that molecular hydrogen cells can effectively filter specific portions of stellar lines, such as the Lyman-$\alpha$ line.

Recent developments show that pre-trained language models have achieved significant success in entity mention typing (EMR). However, existing studies largely focus on the mentions themselves, often overlooking the crucial context surrounding them. To address this, we introduce **FGNET-RF** (Mention Typing with Context and Cross-Context), a new framework designed to integrate context into the mentions and then utilize inter-matching context as input. First, mentions are refined through a bidirectional attention mechanism, allowing the model to focus on key context details. Next, mention representations are enhanced by integrating context information, enabling better understanding of complex semantic cues. Furthermore, mention pairs are refined by leveraging mutual relationships between different sets of mentions, allowing the framework to capture global semantic cues and improve the accuracy and efficiency of the model. Extensive experiments on two public datasets (Mention Typing with Context and Mention Typing with Context) confirm the effectiveness of our approach. Finally, ablation studies provide insights into the impact of various components on model performance.

This research defines the class $\mathcal{U}_\alpha$ of analytic univalent functions in the unit disk $\mathbb{U} = \{u : |u| < 1\}$ via the subordination $g(u) \in \mathbb{U}(a,b,c,\beta)$. It establishes key properties for $g \in \mathcal{U}_\alpha$, including bounds for function coefficients, the Neumann criterion for convexity, hyperbolic traits, and the existence of a radial limit on the unit boundary. Additionally, the Neisnholtz theorem holds for functions within this class.

VM migration serves as a central mechanism in managing cloud data centers, enabling scheduled adjustments to address issues like energy efficiency and load balancing. The primary challenge arises when scheduling these operations sequentially; standard execution often fails to account for the necessity of pre-allocating resources for the migration itself, leading to a situation where critical tasks lack available space and required actions are blocked. To resolve this, this study introduces "Prepartition," an innovative method designed to schedule VMs specifically to minimize both the number of migrations and total power consumption while ensuring those migrations occur without disrupting service. Functioning within a framework that designates a reserved space for migration activities, Prepartition allocates an appropriate amount of memory for each task's move and configures its timing, all while respecting constraints regarding CPU usage, load constraints, and scheduling windows. The method employs a novel sequential scheduling strategy that utilizes a predictive analysis of CPU usage patterns to make informed allocation decisions. Extensive testing across both synthetic and real-world data sets confirms that Prepartition successfully delivers more optimal resource allocations compared to existing techniques, achieving a 10% to 15% reduction in power draw and up to a 20% decrease in migration counts, all while maintaining an acceptable framework for concurrent migrations.

Predicting game-theoretic equilibria is a highly valuable yet challenging endeavor. Conventional single-input-output models like neural networks often fail because they lack the capacity to effectively model interactions among multiple agents. In this paper, we introduce Nash Fixed-Point Networks (N-FPNs), which utilize the principles of fixed-point theory to anticipate these equilibria and leverage the structured interactions between units within a multi-agent neural network framework. Our findings indicate two primary advantages of N-FPNs: (1) they predict multi-agent game equilibria with superior accuracy compared to other state-of-the-art models, and (2) they exhibit enhanced interpretability by mapping agent interactions onto the network's architecture. Furthermore, this approach is adaptable to various input types, including tabular data, images, and text.

Dimensionality reduction techniques have been integrated into causal analysis to construct lower-dimensional representations of confounders, offering a balance between the bias reduction achieved by marginal reduction and the full information power of including all confounders in models that is at an expense of higher dimensionality. However, quantifying the impact of these reduced dimensions on specific causal effects remains a critical challenge. This paper addresses this by introducing a variance decomposition approach to the reduced bias in causal estimands. This approach extends reduction algorithms, such as Principal Component Analysis, by incorporating prior distributions for the transformation weights. Quantitative and simulation results indicate that using a Prior Distribution for weights yields more efficient estimands than standard PCA. Furthermore, we demonstrate how a specific variant of the enhanced PCA can automatically select the optimal number of components to include in causal models, effectively resolving the dilemma between underfitting and overfitting.

This study puts forward a straightforward and quick method for real-time monitoring designed to detect stealthy attacks within model predictive control systems operating under partial information constraints. The core methodology employs a learned estimator to construct relevant features for a supervised classifier, which subsequently operates on reduced-dimensional inputs for enhanced efficiency. To further streamline online operations, the process for generating feature weights is conducted fully analytically and learned beforehand using a non-backpropagation algorithm. Once the classifier is deployed, the approach successfully identifies subtle threats that traditional techniques might overlook, significantly lowering the rate of false positives during runtime.

This paper presents GAE-ISumm, a novel architecture for summarization that integrates graph-based autoencoders with intra-sentence graph structures and utilizes an attention-driven decoder. To address limitations found in traditional autoencoder models, which often fail to adequately capture diverse document relationships, our proposed system constructs a graph to represent multi-dimensional document patterns. Additionally, an intra-sentence graph is created to encode fine-grained sentence relationships, with an attention-based decoder then generating the summary from these relational cues. The attention decoder functions by dynamically focusing on specific relational groups within the sentence graph. Empirical evaluations on standard summarization benchmarks confirm that GAE-ISumm surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in performance. The accompanying source code and pre-trained models can be accessed via https://github.com/zhengzha/GAE-Isumm.

Future instruments like the upcoming \textit{Extremely Large Telescope} instrument MICADO are expected to enable the discovery and characterization of terrestrial planets orbiting solar-type stars at Earth-equivalent distances (A.U.). Additionally, these instruments will facilitate the detailed study of nearby stellar neighbors, including exoplanet host stars, binary systems, and objects within the local galactic environment. However, instrumental limitations such as detector nonlinearity, the finite signal-to-noise ratio, and the inability to perfectly correct atmospheric turbulence-induced distortions introduce complexities that challenge the precision of astrometric and photometric measurements. This study aims to quantify these performance limits for \textit{ELT}/MICADO, specifically evaluating the accuracy of relative astrometry and photometry. The findings indicate that \textit{micron}-level precision in astrometry and \textit{milliJansky} sensitivity in photometry are achievable. The paper also outlines the specific conditions and methodologies necessary to reach these \textit{micron}-scale levels of accuracy.

A primary application of unsupervised learning is discovering meaningful data representations. Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are a widely adopted approach for achieving this, operating by simultaneously modeling latent variable distributions and decoding from that distribution. During VAE training, a standard objective is to optimize the balance between maximizing the likelihood of the observed data and minimizing the complexity of the learned generative model. This study examines the trade-off mechanism within standard VAEs, a component critical to their functionality. We introduce a novel metric for quantifying this balance and evaluate it across four distinct models. Findings indicate that 90% of studies utilizing VAEs lack empirical assessment of this trade-off in 90% of cases, yet our analysis demonstrates a strong correlation between models scoring high on this metric and achieving better performance on downstream tasks. This suggests that current VAE evaluations often prioritize likelihood and overlook the inherent complexity, which significantly impacts subsequent task performance. We anticipate that this work will encourage the research community to monitor this trade-off explicitly and integrate it into metrics that better reflect the true complexity of generative models.

Trilateration based on trilateration is a positioning method that estimates the distance between the transmitter and the receiver to determine the receiver's coordinates. In this study, we propose a deep learning model utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to enhance the accuracy of this process in indoor environments. The research specifically addresses the challenges of obtaining accurate location estimates in indoor settings, where Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) values are often corrupted by noise and signal attenuation from obstacles such as walls. By applying convolutional neural networks, the study improves the performance of existing trilateration methods, achieving superior results compared to approaches relying solely on raw CNNs. While certain neural network architectures aim to express uncertainty in classification, such as through Bayesian methods, they often fail to handle noise robustly. EnCEP couples ensemble modeling with corrective loss correction to better classify noisy data and estimate reliable uncertainty. Specifically, EnCEp leverages diverse model ensembles to assign classification probabilities to training samples. These predictions are then used to identify samples with high uncertainty (low confidence) to prioritize them for correction. By applying a loss function that pushes the model to output lower probabilities for these high-uncertainty samples while increasing probabilities for low-uncertainty ones, we actively steer the model away from erroneous predictions. We evaluated this approach on various datasets, including standard classification benchmarks with artificially introduced label noise. Results demonstrate that ensembles paired with loss correction significantly outperform both other noise-robust methods and standard uncertainty frameworks.

We introduce a method for calculating the partial entanglement of multi-photon wavefunctions within a single spatial mode, contingent on their polarizations. Methodologically, this entanglement is characterized by the energy required to separate the photons from one another. Our numerical analysis of functions describing entanglement versus subsystem size ($K$) relative to the total photon number ($N$) shows that, at small scales, entanglement is negligible compared to $N$, but it approaches significant levels when $K$ nears $N$.

Linear methods are typically employed to derive latent factors from gene expression data, followed by clustering based on their loadings; however, these approaches rely on the assumption that all included variables are predictive, which is often unrealistic. Leveraging relevance learning to filter variables is a more viable strategy for identifying the true drivers of data variation and enhancing the interpretability of the resulting clusters. This study introduces a novel model that combines relevance learning with dynamic factor modeling to dynamically analyze time-dependent gene expression datasets. This methodology dynamically captures the evolution of latent factors and their associated loadings across time, simultaneously inferring gene co-expression networks and their temporal linkages. Crucially, relevance learning allows the model to distinguish the key variables responsible for network structure and latent factor dynamics, thereby reducing noise from non-informative variables. Additionally, because the model is formulated as a hierarchical structure, it facilitates parallelization for high-performance computing and can be extended to handle high-sparsity environments through integrated penalty terms. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method effectively selects genes and yields accurate estimates of factor and loading trajectories across various scenarios. Finally, empirical analysis was conducted on mouse embryonic stem cell data to examine the dynamic behavior of cell-to-cell variability during self-renewal.

Although recurrent neural networks (RNs) function effectively for tasks involving inference and learning, their internal hidden states remain difficult to interpret. This study investigates an original class of continuous-time Markov processes—Hidden Markov Processes (HMPs)—which encompass both recurrent and linear dynamical systems. We demonstrate that within an optimal control context regarding one-dimensional beliefs, the evolution of these recurrent state variables aligns exactly with a Bayesian filter's performance. Furthermore, we establish that the trajectories of the beliefs regarding the system's state mirror the time-evolved observability Gramian of associated linear dynamical systems. These findings offer a concrete interpretation of the internal machinery in recurrent architectures, suggesting they are optimized for preserving reduced-dimensional beliefs under the principle of minimum entropy production.

Although existing video-based action detection methods have achieved significant success, current models often rely on laborious manual annotation of keyframes and frames to ensure high performance. This study proposes a end-to-end architecture that utilizes Self-Attention mechanisms and Graph Convolutional Networks to identify actions directly from video frames. The resulting framework is more efficient and effective in processing large-scale video datasets. The effectiveness of the proposed method is further validated through experimental results conducted on the UCF100 and HMDB51 benchmarks.

Current image-based copy detection techniques typically rely on extensive handcrafted algorithms, including local feature extraction, clustering to generate a feature bag, pose estimation, copy-paste preprocessing like black-and-white conversion, and specific evaluation metrics. This study introduces a straightforward, unsupervised deep learning approach for detecting copied images, minimizing reliance on these manual components by converting input images into local Gabor filters and feeding them into a pre-trained convolutional neural network to extract features. These extracted features are then aggregated into a bag using mean pooling, with an additional copy-paste purification process applied before these filtered features enhance detection accuracy. Experiments conducted on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance; notably, a variant lacking the copy-paste purification step still surpasses existing methods, indicating that deep learning-extracted features offer superior quality over traditional handcrafted ones.

Table extraction involves retrieving data tables from document visuals and structuring them into tabular formats, a complex task complicated by diverse source domains, varying visual layouts, and different output requirements. We suggest a method that unifies multiple previous hypotheses into a singular framework by leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to address the challenging problem of table extraction from visual documents. This approach decouples the task into two streamlined sub-tasks: outlining potential table cells through ground graph analysis and predicting boundary boxes via skip connections derived directly from cell features; critical decisions regarding the network architecture and strategy were informed by analysis of state-of-the-art research and anomalies detected in recent benchmarks. Empirical evidence confirms that this proposed methodology surpasses the performance of current leading techniques.

Dynamic games are characterized by evolving network structures of cooperation, where interactions occur across networks that transform over time. This study proposes an adaptive network dynamics framework based on three primary mechanisms: network switching, group formation, and inter-group competition. Players operate within higher-level groups composed of both higher-level and lower-level participants; each player attempts to maximize their payoff by adopting face types, which dictate their ability to access social information. Specifically, lower-level players are confined to simpler face models (e.g., primary or secondary faces), whereas higher-level players can examine deeper social networks and evaluate more complex hierarchies (e.g., tertiary or quaternary faces). Research findings indicate that lower-level players, possessing less comprehensive social network knowledge, tend to exhibit higher adaptability in their network choices. Conversely, higher-level players, with broader social network insights, are predicted to be more inclined toward clustering with homogeneous group members. Furthermore, the study reveals that introducing heterogeneous group structures enhances system resilience against network attacks and improves overall payoff outcomes. This paper introduces an accurate methodology for generating population predictions by leveraging satellite imagery of urban regions. Our central approach involves employing these images to calculate footprint areas—contiguous high-resolution images representing a specific population density at a certain scale—and utilizing these derived features to enhance the predictive model. The study's primary contribution lies in creating novel estimation techniques that rely on a publicly available, location-specific distance to a major highway as the sole auxiliary feature. This feature is then contrasted with combinations involving additional private features from the Google GeoMind Challenge dataset to evaluate their comparative predictive power. Furthermore, we conduct an extensive ablation study to analyze the sensitivity of our results regarding the chosen public feature and the selected convolutional kernel sizes. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that incorporating estimated footprint areas substantially improves prediction performance surpassing models built solely on limited open-source inputs, and both ablation analysis and visual examinations provide meaningful insights valuable for researchers engaged in similar population prediction tasks.

We introduce a novel filter type, "static filters," to which queries are not submitted, ensuring no false positives. By eliminating the overhead of maintaining a dynamic data structure, these filters achieve an order of magnitude more than standard speed and space complexities compared to traditional methods, all while guaranteeing a zero false-positive rate. Our approach is further supported by advanced techniques that enable precise estimation of the commonality of random subsets within their filter.

We demonstrate that a one-dimensional atom-molecule setup comprising a two-level atom and its harmonically trapped ground-state molecular partner is driven by a *quasi*-resonant laser to effectively behave as a non-rigid piston. In this analogy, the atom serves as the point mass pendulum while the transition energy between ground and excited states acts as an adjustable bond length. Near the half Rabi frequency condition, the pendulum's dynamics serve as an effective single-particle model, enabling the characterization of atomic resonance conditions and the emergence of quantum instabilities. Within this non-rigid effective theory, quantum non-classicality is observed in the atom whenever the effective bond length is shorter than the corresponding classical minimum. The model is applicable to trapped ground-state molecular systems and potentially various other platforms, offering significant promise for the coherent generation of non-classical atoms from the starting point of molecules.

We introduce a novel multi-resolution computational hydrodynamics (MPH) framework that integrates a phase model to handle significant density variations and the prevention of vacuities. Utilizing a multi-phase approach, we assign a dominant phase with high density alongside a light tracer phase; the latter's density evolves according to advection equations, with its initial state mirroring the relative concentration of the two substances. This strategy effectively resolves void formation inherent in single-phase density re-initialization schemes and allows independent temporal resolution of phases with distinct densities, avoiding the computational overhead of resolving the dominant phase for tracer-level details. Within the MPH framework, a polytropic equation of state is applied to the high-density phase, while the tracer phase receives an artificial, equation-of-state-independent density to maintain spatial resolution accuracy. This advancement has been validated through benchmark tests on Rayleigh-Taylor and Richtmyer-Meshkov instabilities, demonstrating strong agreement with theoretical predictions and prior research across varying density ratios.

K-means clustering stands out as a widely utilized unsupervised learning algorithm in data analysis. This study introduces a quantum k-means protocol featuring asymptotic speedup, which is more efficient than existing quantum clustering solutions. This method is designed to handle large datasets split into a set of $N$ clusters, where each point exists as a quantum state, and the full matrix of these points is not memory-accessible. K-means traditionally relies on identifying the centroid of a specific distribution, making this algorithm adaptive rather than adaptive; specifically, it generates new data points—potentially referred to as an oracular set of data points—to be inserted into an evolving set of data points. This dynamic data generation is intended to converge toward an approximation of the target distribution's true centroid, which our theory demonstrates has improved convergence properties over classical methods. Additionally, we show that this algorithm can be extended to learn the mean vector of a distribution from an unobservable matrix of points.

Current end-to-side object-centric spatiotemporal models face a challenge: the vast search space created by object-centric reasoning, now further expanded by time, leads to a significant delay in convergence. To address this, we propose a strategy that suppresses the decoding of object features, thereby delaying their reconstruction from the encoded space until feature representations are learned more effectively. This approach is supported by a contrastive loss function that pulls together consistent object features while pushing apart inconsistent ones, effectively reducing a complex scene into its essential components. Evaluations on the MVS-Mind dataset confirm that this simplified, delayed decoding framework converges substantially faster than previous methods, achieving a 30% reduction in training duration with comparable accuracy to top-performing baseline models.

The transverse-momentum ($p_T$) distribution of lepton pairs serves as a critical observable in charged-current (CC) Drell-Yan processes, undergoing substantial evolution across the spectrum of lepton pair transverse momenta. Consequently, accurate simulation models of this observable are essential for precise theoretical predictions and reliable uncertainty assessments in high-$p_T$ CC events at hadron colliders. This precision heavily depends upon the proper tuning of underlying simulation frameworks, particularly reg格onization models which dominate at high lepton pair $p_T$. This analysis examines the relation between the experimental CC $p_T$ distribution and the underlying parton kinematics and subsequent simulation choices concerning shower evolution and initial state radiation. Furthermore, we evaluate the sensitivity of these distributions to the tuning parameters embedded within the Monte Carlo tools. By quantifying these dependencies, we establish the foundation for a systematic tuning procedure for high-$p_T$ charged-current simulative scenarios.

Telepresence robots are increasingly prevalent in both research and practical settings, with a growing focus on enhancing user experience (UX). To investigate this area, a mixed-method approach was employed, combining surveys with telepresence robot usage sessions. The study involved 120 participants who completed surveys regarding their perceptions of the robot, followed by practical navigation and control tasks. Survey responses revealed significant disparities in how participants view visual aspects versus navigation/control functionalities of the system. Furthermore, analysis identified distinct user categories based on navigation and control experiences. Navigation performance was objectively measured using robot trajectories, navigation scores, and error counts. Additionally, questionnaires administered during these tasks gathered subjective UX data.

This research examines hierarchical models utilizing linear and generalized linear frameworks, featuring quantiles as response variables across four distinct case studies. The first case involves fitting a quantile regression model to data regarding forest tree volume, where fitted results are contrasted with those from traditional linear regression methods. Cases 2 and 3 utilize a quantile regression approach on ecological dataset regarding plants, addressing nitrogen soil levels as the predictor for plant biomass size; subsequently, these results are compared against findings from case 4, which employs multivariate quantile regression on data measuring both the length and width of fish otoliths alongside concentrations of mercury and PCBs. The final analysis contrasts quantile regression outcomes with those of multivariate regression techniques. Throughout the study, diagnostic measures assess model appropriateness, while quantitative evidence supports rejecting null hypotheses in cases 2 and 4.

This paper investigates the game Mafia by formally establishing its state space and defining the state transition functions that correspond to the various ruleset components. By utilizing a Markov chain framework to analyze this state-machine representation, the study derives the steady-state distribution of the state function. This approach provides a quantitative assessment of key game metrics, including average duration and time spent within specific states, while the distribution itself reveals the system's time-scale. By linking these metrics to player groupings and initial starting ratios through simulation experiments, the paper formulates a unified expression that connects game length to participant composition and player roles.

Recent observations indicate that giant planets are more likely to have a "Jupiter-like" composition than a "core-dominant" one, a distribution that remains unexplained. This study explores whether multiple giant planets, formed simultaneously from the same disk, can acquire similar masses and, by extension, comparable internal structures. The authors present a method to derive the initial disk properties required for multiple planets to match a specific set of starting conditions. In scenarios without migration, the convergence of masses occurs naturally: outer planets lose their gas disks more slowly than inner planets due to temperature gradients, causing both groups to reach a consistent equilibrium gap width and resulting in divergent final masses. The resulting distribution shows an inner-planet "convention" tending toward lower masses than the outer set. Furthermore, when migration influences orbital evolution, the mass spread can be minimized even more. The paper concludes that this mechanism offers a plausible explanation for the lack of "core-heavy" giant planets in the galaxy.

At low temperatures, a logarithmic variation of the resistivity with temperature is observed, which serves as evidence of weak localization. Furthermore, a comparison between the predicted and the actual temperature dependence of the resistivity is made, which shows a good agreement.

The SAGES project utilizes the VLT/X-shooter instrument to gather near-infrared (0.9$-$\sim$ 2.4 $\mu$m) spectra for a high-resolution 3D study of the globular cluster NGC 6441. The initial findings focus on a sample of blue horizontal branch stars positioned near the cluster center, analyzing their spectral features to determine kinematics and abundances. The study reveals that these stars belong to distinct sub-populations characterized by differing metal abundances and space velocities; these groups are spatially segregated and likely represent distinct accretion events. Furthermore, individual stellar abundances are calculated for several elements, including Ca, Mg, Al, Si, S, Ca, and Fe, with future investigations planned for heavier elements like Ne, Na, K, and the odd-Z elements. The results show a trend of enhanced odd-element abundances alongside even-Z depletion in the cluster's central regions. Future SAGES phases will explore the full cluster volume and examine these chemical kinematics across an extended sample of horizontal branch and red giant stars.

Transfer learning is a standard practice in machine learning that relies on reusing previously trained models to accelerate training on new tasks. However, understanding which components of a deep neural network (DNN) can be effectively transferred to novel domains remains unclear. While basic features like edges and shapes are typically associated with early layers, and later layers appear more domain-specific, the actual location of transferable components within a DNN has not been definitively established. This study aims to resolve this by analyzing feature representations across different layers to determine where critical, transferable information resides. We propose that the primary factors enabling successful transfer are invariant basic features (such as edges and corners) combined with common high-level semantic patterns. To measure information transfer, we define a new entropy-based metric and demonstrate that features at every layer contribute to the transferable knowledge base. Furthermore, by evaluating the information present in each layer, we successfully identify the most transferable layer for a specific new class within a new domain, successfully testing our approach across image and audio datasets.

The primary challenge of employing a single unified model across diverse datasets lies in the difficulty of establishing causal links between cause-and-effect variables due to various interference factors, including confounders. To address dependency issues, we introduce the Backward Dropped Algorithm (BDA), which selectively discards redundant data points that obscure long-term dependency patterns. Following this, we present the Causal Inference by BDA (CIBDA) framework, which combines BDA with a novel Causal Inference Network (CIN) to identify causalities. Our approach features a forward selection mechanism for network construction, an entropy-based entropy maximization (EMIE) method for determining causal strength, and a scheme for establishing causal directionality. Finally, a hierarchical causal graph is established to summarize findings. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm the efficacy of our proposed approach.

This approach allows for the assessment of the model's performance on out-of-distribution data sets in practical settings.
